title: K-Means Clustering & the Elbow Method

blocks.t: From the notes
K-Means, as written

Unsupervised — there is no output column. We only have $X$,
and we group similar points together.
Steps:

items: Assign each point to the nearest centroid (Euclidean distance).
Move each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it.
Repeat 3 and 4 until the centroids stop moving.

blocks.t:
How to choose k — the Elbow Method. Plot WCSS (within
cluster sum of squares) against $k$. WCSS keeps decreasing; we pick the
point where the graph bends like an elbow.
Feature scaling required.

blocks.cap:
Five iterations of Lloyd's algorithm from a random start. The crosses
are centroids. Each panel reports the WCSS, which falls monotonically until the
assignment stops changing.

blocks.t: The objective, and why the two steps are what they are
K-Means minimises the within-cluster sum of squares:
\boxed{ \text{WCSS} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{i \in C_j} \|x_i-\mu_j\|^2 }

over both the assignment $\{C_j\}$ and the centroids $\{\mu_j\}$. This is a
joint optimisation over a discrete variable and a continuous one, and it is
NP-hard in general. Lloyd's algorithm solves it by coordinate descent
— fix one, optimise the other, alternate.

Step A (assignment), centroids fixed. WCSS decomposes into a sum over
points, and each point contributes $\|x_i-\mu_{j(i)}\|^2$ independently.
Minimising a sum of independent terms means minimising each: send every point to
its nearest centroid. That is step 3 of the notes.

Step B (update), assignment fixed. For cluster $j$ we minimise
$g(\mu)=\sum_{i\in C_j}\|x_i-\mu\|^2$. Differentiate:

\nabla g = -2\sum_{i\in C_j}(x_i-\mu) = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu_j = \frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{i\in C_j} x_i .

The mean is not a heuristic — it is the exact minimiser of squared
distance. That is step 4.
Why it converges

Both steps weakly decrease the same objective, so WCSS is
non-increasing. There are only finitely many possible assignments ($k^n$), and
the objective strictly decreases whenever the assignment changes. Therefore the
algorithm cannot cycle and must terminate in a finite number of steps.

But it converges to a local minimum, not the global one. Which one you
get depends entirely on the initialisation — see the histogram in the last
figure.

Because the objective is squared Euclidean distance, K-Means is tied to
that metric: substituting an arbitrary distance breaks the proof that the mean
is optimal. If you need another metric, use K-Medoids
(minimises an arbitrary distance to an actual data point, robust to outliers,
much slower) or K-Modes for categorical data.
Choosing k

blocks.cap:
Left: the elbow. Middle: the silhouette score, which unlike WCSS has a
genuine maximum. Right: the per-point silhouette plot for $k=4$.

blocks.t:
The elbow method's weakness. WCSS decreases monotonically with $k$ —
at $k=n$ it is exactly zero, with every point its own cluster. So there is no
optimum to find; you are eyeballing a change in curvature, and on real data the
curve is usually smooth with no obvious bend. Two people will read two different
elbows off the same plot.

The silhouette coefficient gives a real, maximisable criterion. For
point $i$:
a_i = \text{mean distance to the other points in its own cluster},
b_i = \min_{j \neq \text{own}} \text{mean distance to all points in cluster } j,
s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)} \in [-1, 1].

$s_i \approx 1$: well inside its cluster. $s_i \approx 0$: on the boundary
between two clusters. $s_i < 0$: closer on average to another cluster than to
its own — probably misassigned. The overall score is $\bar s$, and we choose
the $k$ that maximises it.

blocks.t: Initialisation and k-means++

blocks.cap:
Left: 40 random seeds with n_init=1. Purely random
initialisation lands in bad local optima; k-means++ almost never does. Middle
and right: the same data with one feature scaled by 60, before and after
standardisation.

blocks.t: k-means++ chooses the seeds to be spread out:

items: Pick the first centre uniformly at random from the data.

For every point compute $D(x)$ = distance to the nearest already
chosen centre.

Pick the next centre from the data with probability proportional to
$D(x)^2$.
Repeat until $k$ centres are chosen, then run Lloyd's algorithm.

blocks.t:
The $D(x)^2$ weighting makes far-away points overwhelmingly likely to be
chosen, so seeds land in different clusters. This guarantees an expected WCSS
within $O(\log k)$ of the global optimum — a rare theoretical guarantee for a
clustering method, and it is sklearn's default.

Always leave n_init at 10 or more (sklearn $\ge$1.4 defaults to
n_init="auto", which is 1 with k-means++ and 10 with random init).
Each restart is a fresh initialisation; the run with the lowest WCSS is kept.
Setting n_init=1 to save time is the most common way to get a silently
bad clustering.
Where K-Means fails

blocks.cap:
The four canonical failure modes. All follow from one fact: minimising
squared Euclidean distance to a centre implicitly assumes spherical, equally
sized, equally dense clusters.

head: Failure
Why
What to use instead
rows: Cluster regions are Voronoi cells — always convex polytopes
A large diffuse cluster has high WCSS, so the objective prefers to split it
Distance is isotropic; it cannot see a covariance
The mean is not robust; one far point drags a centroid

blocks.t:
K-Means is the hard-assignment, equal-spherical-covariance special case
of a Gaussian mixture model fitted by EM. Assignment is the E-step made
deterministic; the mean update is the M-step. Seeing it this way makes the
failure modes obvious: relax to full covariances and elongated clusters work;
relax to soft assignment and boundary points stop being forced into one side.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, MiniBatchKMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import (silhouette_score, silhouette_samples,
                             calinski_harabasz_score, davies_bouldin_score,
                             adjusted_rand_score)

X, y_true = make_blobs(n_samples=1500, centers=4, cluster_std=1.0, random_state=7)

# ==================================================================
# 1. LLOYD'S ALGORITHM FROM SCRATCH -- the whole thing is two lines in a loop
# ==================================================================
def kmeans(X, k, iters=100, tol=1e-6, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]        # naive init
    for it in range(iters):
        # --- ASSIGN: every point to its nearest centroid ---------------
        d2  = ((X[:, None, :] - C[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)   # (n, k)
        lab = d2.argmin(axis=1)
        wcss = d2.min(axis=1).sum()

        # --- UPDATE: every centroid to the mean of its cluster ---------
        newC = np.array([X[lab == j].mean(axis=0) if (lab == j).any() else C[j]
                         for j in range(k)])
        shift = np.linalg.norm(newC - C)
        C = newC
        if shift < tol:                                # centroids stopped moving
            break
    return C, lab, wcss, it + 1

C, lab, wcss, n_it = kmeans(X, 4, seed=3)
print(f"converged in {n_it} iterations, WCSS = {wcss:.1f}")

km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("sklearn inertia_ (= WCSS):", round(km.inertia_, 1))
print("agreement with scratch:", round(adjusted_rand_score(lab, km.labels_), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 2. k-means++ INITIALISATION, BY HAND
# ==================================================================
def kmeanspp(X, k, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    C = [X[rng.integers(len(X))]]                      # first centre: uniform
    for _ in range(k - 1):
        D2 = np.min(((X[:, None, :] - np.array(C)[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
        probs = D2 / D2.sum()                          # proportional to D(x)^2
        C.append(X[rng.choice(len(X), p=probs)])
    return np.array(C)

# Measured: how much better than random seeding?
rand_w = [KMeans(4, init="random",    n_init=1, random_state=s).fit(X).inertia_
          for s in range(30)]
pp_w   = [KMeans(4, init="k-means++", n_init=1, random_state=s).fit(X).inertia_
          for s in range(30)]
print(f"random init : mean {np.mean(rand_w):8.1f}  worst {max(rand_w):8.1f}")
print(f"k-means++   : mean {np.mean(pp_w):8.1f}  worst {max(pp_w):8.1f}")

# ==================================================================
# 3. CHOOSING k -- four criteria at once
# ==================================================================
print(f"{'k':>3} {'WCSS':>10} {'silhouette':>11} {'CH':>9} {'DB':>7}")
for k in range(2, 9):
    m = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
    print(f"{k:3d} {m.inertia_:10.1f} {silhouette_score(X, m.labels_):11.4f} "
          f"{calinski_harabasz_score(X, m.labels_):9.1f} "
          f"{davies_bouldin_score(X, m.labels_):7.3f}")
# WCSS never stops falling. Silhouette and CH peak; DB is minimised.

# Elbow located programmatically -- the "knee": maximum distance from the
# straight line joining the first and last point of the curve.
ks = np.arange(1, 11)
w  = np.array([KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X).inertia_ for k in ks])
p1, p2 = np.array([ks[0], w[0]]), np.array([ks[-1], w[-1]])
line = p2 - p1
dists = np.abs(np.cross(line, np.column_stack([ks, w]) - p1)) / np.linalg.norm(line)
print("elbow at k =", ks[dists.argmax()])

# ==================================================================
# 4. SCALING -- inside a pipeline, always
# ==================================================================
Xu = X.copy(); Xu[:, 1] *= 60                    # one feature in different units
print("unscaled ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(
      y_true, KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xu)), 3))
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0))
print("scaled   ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(y_true, pipe.fit_predict(Xu)), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 5. PREDICTING, TRANSFORMING, AND THE CENTROIDS AS FEATURES
# ==================================================================
km = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("centres:\n", km.cluster_centers_.round(2))
print("assign new points:", km.predict([[0, 0], [5, 5]]))
# transform() gives the distance to every centroid -- a useful k-dimensional
# feature for a downstream supervised model ("cluster distance features").
print("distance features shape:", km.transform(X[:3]).round(2))

# ==================================================================
# 6. SCALING TO LARGE n -- MiniBatchKMeans
# ==================================================================
Xbig, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=500000, centers=8, random_state=0)
mb = MiniBatchKMeans(n_clusters=8, batch_size=2048, n_init=5,
                     random_state=0).fit(Xbig)
print("minibatch inertia:", round(mb.inertia_, 1))
# Updates centroids from small random batches. Roughly an order of magnitude
# faster, with slightly worse WCSS. Supports partial_fit for streaming.

# ==================================================================
# 7. SILHOUETTE DIAGNOSTICS -- find the badly-placed points
# ==================================================================
s = silhouette_samples(X, km.labels_)
print("points with negative silhouette:", int((s < 0).sum()))
for j in range(4):
    print(f"cluster {j}: n={np.sum(km.labels_ == j):4d}  mean s={s[km.labels_ == j].mean():.3f}")
Everything on one page
Summary

Objective: minimise WCSS $=\sum_j\sum_{i\in C_j}\|x_i-\mu_j\|^2$.
NP-hard exactly; Lloyd's algorithm is coordinate descent on it.

Two steps: assign each point to the nearest centroid (optimal for
fixed $\mu$); move each centroid to its cluster mean (the exact minimiser of
squared distance). Both decrease WCSS, so it always converges — to a
local optimum.

Initialisation matters. Use k-means++ and n_init $\ge$
10.

Choosing k: elbow on WCSS (monotone, ambiguous), silhouette
(has a real maximum, $O(n^2)$), Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin, gap
statistic, or domain knowledge.
Scale first. Distance in mixed units is meaningless.

Assumes spherical, equal-sized, equal-density clusters. Fails on
moons, elongated clusters, unequal densities, and outliers. It is the
hard-assignment, isotropic special case of a Gaussian mixture.

Complexity: $O(n k d i)$ per run — fast and linear in $n$. Use
MiniBatchKMeans above a few hundred thousand rows.
Interview corner
Q. Explain K-Means in three sentences.

Pick $k$ centroids, assign every point to its nearest one, then move each
centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it, and repeat until nothing
moves. Each step provably lowers the within-cluster sum of squares, so it
converges. The result is a local optimum that depends on the initial centroids.
Q. Why the mean, and not the median?

Because the objective is squared Euclidean distance, whose minimiser is
the mean. With absolute distance the minimiser is the median — that is
K-Medians, and it is more robust to outliers.
Q. Does K-Means always converge? To the best answer?

It always converges, because both steps weakly decrease a bounded objective and
there are finitely many assignments. It does not converge to the global
optimum — the problem is NP-hard, and different seeds give different local
optima. Mitigate with k-means++ and multiple restarts.
Q. Weakness of the elbow method?

WCSS decreases monotonically and reaches zero at $k=n$, so there is no maximum
or minimum to find — you are visually detecting a change of slope, which is
subjective and often absent on real data. Silhouette or the gap statistic give
an actual optimum.
Q. What is the silhouette coefficient?

$s_i=(b_i-a_i)/\max(a_i,b_i)$, where $a_i$ is the mean distance to points in
its own cluster and $b_i$ the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. It
combines cohesion and separation, ranges over $[-1,1]$, and negative values flag
probable misassignments.
Q. Why does K-Means fail on the two-moons dataset?

Because it assigns points to the nearest centroid, the clusters are Voronoi
cells — always convex. A crescent is not convex and cannot be a Voronoi cell,
so K-Means cuts both moons in half. Use DBSCAN or spectral clustering.
Q. How does k-means++ work and why is it better?

It picks seeds one at a time with probability proportional to the squared
distance to the nearest already-chosen seed, so centres start far apart and in
different clusters. It guarantees an expected WCSS within $O(\log k)$ of
optimal, and empirically both converges faster and finds better optima.
Q. Relationship to Gaussian mixture models?

K-Means is the limiting case of a GMM fitted by EM with hard assignments and
shared spherical covariance $\sigma^2 I$ as $\sigma\to0$. GMMs allow soft
memberships and per-cluster full covariances, which is why they handle
elongated and overlapping clusters that K-Means cannot.
Q. How do you cluster categorical or mixed data?

Not with K-Means — the mean of categories is undefined. Use K-Modes
(categorical), K-Prototypes (mixed), hierarchical clustering with Gower
distance, or embed the categories first.
Q. How would you evaluate a clustering when you do have labels?

Adjusted Rand Index or Normalised Mutual Information — both are invariant to
label permutation, which raw accuracy is not. Without labels, use internal
measures (silhouette, Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin) plus stability under
resampling.
Worked Examples
K-Means by hand, two iterations
Iteration 1 – assign. Each point joins its nearest centroid.
Update. New centroids are the means of each cluster:

Iteration 2 – assign again. Distance from $B=(2,1)$ to $c_1=(1.333,1.333)$ is $\sqrt{0.667^2+0.333^2} = 0.75$, versus $\sqrt{3.333^2+4.333^2} = 5.47$ to $c_2$. No point changes cluster, so the algorithm has converged.
Inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) at convergence:
\sum_{\text{clusters}}\sum_{x} \|x - c\|^2 = 2.667
Why the result depends on initialisation. Starting from $c_1=(1,1)$ and $c_2=(1,5)$ instead can converge elsewhere on other data. That is why KMeans uses n_init restarts and the k-means++ seeding.
